tier_reason: The original benchmark_url (rust-leipzig/regex-performance chart) states flags (CMake Release -O3 -march=native) and hardware but not the compiler, so on its own it would be B (independent third-party suite). The independent mariomka/regex-benchmark meets A in full: in-repo code cpp/benchmark.cpp built by run-benchmarks.php as 'g++ -std=c++11 -O3' (with and without -DUSE_BOOST), g++ 7.5.0 / Boost 1.65.1 stated, and the hardware stated. benchmark_url was switched to that source.

corrections.claimed_speedup: mariomka/regex-benchmark: C++ Boost 104.23 ms vs C++ STL (std::regex) 1023.49 ms total, ~9.8x (Email 44.97 vs 433.09 ~9.6x; URI 44.13 vs 344.74 ~7.8x; IPv4 15.13 vs 245.66 ~16.2x); the 'optimized' table shows 104.28 vs 1021.10. Supporting evidence from the rust-leipzig/regex-performance chart (results_20221012.png, ms): Boost was faster on 13 of the 14 patterns both engines ran, from ~1.0x ('[a-z]shing' 323.5 vs 326.1) up to ~48.5x ('Tom|Sawyer|Huckleberry|Finn' 12.2 vs 591.3; 'Twain' 8.7 vs 223 ~26x; '\u221E|\u2713' 7.3 vs 340.7 ~47x). It was slower on '([A-Za-z]awyer|[A-Za-z]inn)\s' (800.8 vs 595). On '(.*?,){13}z' std::regex took 17989.3 while Boost was n/a.
corrections.workload: mariomka/regex-benchmark: find and count non-overlapping matches of 3 patterns (Email, URI, IPv4) over a concatenation of the Learn-X-in-Y-minutes docs. The timing includes pattern compilation. Supporting: rust-leipzig regex_perf runs 18 patterns (literal, alternation, character classes, bounded repeats, case-insensitive variants, one catastrophic-backtracking pattern) over 3200.txt (~16 MB). The README says 'best of 5', but src/boost.cpp and src/cppstd.cpp actually record the mean of 5 runs, in ms.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 7.5.0, -std=c++11 -O3, Boost 1.65.1 (mariomka run-benchmarks.php / cpp/README.md). The supporting rust-leipzig run used CMake Release -O3 -march=native with CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -std=c++11; its compiler and version are not stated.
corrections.hardware: MacBook Pro (16-inch, 2019), 2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, 32 GB 2667 MHz DDR4, macOS Big Sur 11.2.3, running a Docker ubuntu:bionic image (mariomka). The supporting rust-leipzig run used an AMD Threadripper 3960X (Zen2) at 3.8 GHz on Ubuntu 20.04.5 LTS.
corrections.caveats: The mariomka numbers are from 2021 (last commit 2021-10-18) with Boost 1.65.1 and libstdc++ from g++ 7.5.0, and its timings include regex compilation. The rust-leipzig chart is PNG-only, does not state the compiler, and its README misdescribes aggregation (says best-of-5, code computes the mean). A third source, c0rp3n/regex-bench (archived, 2 stars, Ryzen 2700X), shows std::regex 44662340 ns vs boost::regex 4875681 ns (~9.2x), with compiler and flags not stated. GitHub reports a null license for boostorg/regex, but the headers carry the Boost Software License 1.0.

notes: The direction (Boost.Regex much faster than libstdc++ std::regex) is confirmed by three independent suites. The original chart numbers check out; the only error was the pattern '\u221e|\u221a', which is actually '\u221E|\u2713' in src/main.c. last_commit on the default branch (develop) is 2026-05-22; 2026-08-13 is the repo's pushed_at, likely from a non-default branch. Still active.

tier_reason: The README table and note state clang 12.0.0 -O2, a 2.9 GHz Intel Core i7 with 16 GB LPDDR3, and Mac OS X 12.6.9. The README's linked 'Download the tests' artifact (genivia.com/files/perfcomp.zip, live) contains the Makefile and sources, including the std::regex leg: target stdecmatest, built from ecmareflextest.l with reflex -m=std-ecma, -std=c++11 -O2.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 8.7 us (reflex --fast --noindent), 8.9 us (--fast) and 20.6 us (--full), all RE/flex 3.4.1, vs 6490 us for std::cregex_iterator() (C++11 std::regex): ~315x-746x faster on this tokenizing workload. In the same table RE/flex --fast also beats PCRE2 JIT (60.8 us), PCRE2 non-JIT (500 us), Boost.Regex perl (205 us), Boost.Regex POSIX (392 us) and RE2 (218 us).
corrections.caveats: This is the author's own benchmark. The harness is an external zip on genivia.com (perfcomp.zip, dated Sept 2023), not committed to the git repo. It was measured with RE/flex 3.4.1, while the repo is now at 6.x. The std::regex figure comes from running std::regex through RE/flex's std-ecma matcher adapter with one large alternation pattern, not a hand-written std::regex loop. libc++ is inferred from macOS/clang, not stated explicitly.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly; the record only garbled the PCRE2 and Boost ranges, now fixed. Metadata verified: BSD-3-Clause, 599 stars, last commit 2026-09-15, not a fork. The README confirms use by ugrep and the Tiger Compiler.

tier_reason: There is reproducible in-repo code (benchmarks/bench_engines.cpp via 'make bench-engines', c++ -std=c++20 -O2) with compilers stated (g++ 13.3.0, Apple clang 16). But hardware is given only as ISA ('x86-64' container, 'arm64' Apple on AC power) with no CPU model, so it fails A. It is a self-published benchmark with no peer review or third-party suite, so not B; C by elimination.

corrections.caveats: This is an extremely new, very small project (4 stars, created 2026-06-13) with no external validation beyond its own suite. The CPU models for both benchmark hosts are not disclosed: the x86-64 leg ran in a container with documented 'episodic interference'. std::regex is 'unsupported' for the anchored row on both ISAs and for the possessive row on arm64, so the std::regex ranges cover 11 (x86-64) and 10 (arm64) of the 12 patterns. BENCHMARKS.md is unusually self-critical: it documents past drift between the summary bullets and the measured tables, and warns that before/after deltas are layout-noise-sensitive.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the §A tables and bullets exactly (8.20-41.97x x86-64, 15.31-151.97x arm64, RE2 2.90-16.34x / 2.41-11.53x, PCRE2-JIT beaten on 7 of 12 on both ISAs). The downgrade is only because the hardware is undisclosed. It would qualify for A if the CPU models were stated. Metadata verified: MIT, 4 stars, last commit 2026-09-24T02:27Z (UTC).

tier_reason: The README shows Google Benchmark output from the in-repo unformat_benchmark.cpp (Unformat 32.6 ns, constexpr 11.5 ns, StdRegex 3269 ns), but the compiler, flags and OS are unstated (only '32 X 2420 MHz CPU s'), and the gain is 100-284x (>50x). That caps it at C.

corrections.workload: Parsing 'Harry is 18 years old and weighs 67.8 kilograms' against '{} is {} years old and weighs {} {}' into string_view, int, float and string_view, timed with Google Benchmark (unformat_benchmark.cpp). The std::regex leg uses regex_search with a 4-group pattern, then stoi/stof and std::string copies. The README usage example '{} is {} years old.' is not the benchmarked input.
corrections.caveats: The StdRegex benchmark constructs (compiles) std::regex inside the timed loop on every iteration, so the 3269 ns includes pattern compilation plus std::string/stoi/stof conversions. That inflates the gap versus a precompiled regex, and the '300x' claim should be read with this in mind. The README does not state the compiler, optimization flags or OS (only 32 x 2420 MHz CPUs). The same run also shows std::stringstream at 391 ns and sscanf at 677 ns. This is typed parsing of a fixed format, narrower than general regex matching.

notes: The numbers match the README; the repo description says 'up to 300x faster than std::regex'. Metadata verified: Unlicense (OSI-approved), 46 stars, last commit 2026-03-02, not a fork. The workload was misdescribed and a significant fairness caveat (regex compiled per iteration) was missing; both are now fixed.

tier_reason: The ESA 2016 paper (peer-reviewed) states g++ 4.8.4 -O3 -march=native and an Intel Core i5-2500K on Ubuntu 14.04.4. The repo holds the reproducible harness (driver.cpp plus makefile targets 'make timetest' / '<alg>.time', CXXFLAGS -O3 -std=c++11 -march=native) timing against the bundled GCC 4.7.2 std::sort copy (stl_gcc).

corrections.claimed_speedup: More than 80% more elements sorted per second than GCC's std::sort on random ints. Section 4: optimized BlockQuicksort needs ~45 ns/element vs 85 ns/element for std::sort at n=2^28 (+88%), and the duplicate-check variant is almost twice as fast on random ints in [0, sqrt n]. Figure 7 shows smaller but positive gains on Vector and Record for the BlockQS (mo-sqrt n, dc) variant. std::sort wins only on sorted or almost-sorted inputs.

notes: The claims, compiler, flags and hardware all match the paper; the old benchmark_url 301-redirects to https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol057-esa2016/LIPIcs.ESA.2016.38/LIPIcs.ESA.2016.38.pdf and still works. Metadata verified: GPL-3.0, 40 stars, last commit 2021-11-29 (>3 years, so abandoned), not archived, not a fork.
